analysis.one_liner: Freezes all new federal rulemaking and repeals every federal rule issued since 1991.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in subcommittees from November 2011 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The STRIP Act would have stopped federal agencies from issuing any new rules for at least two years, except in emergencies or with special sign-offs. More dramatically, it would have repealed every federal rule that took effect after October 1, 1991 — clean air limits, workplace safety standards, food safety rules, benefit rules and more — unless Congress affirmatively reauthorized each one. Only rules affecting banks, tax administration, the military, and trade agreements were carved out.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated businesses, especially those facing environmental, health, or safety rules, would gain the most: nearly two decades of standing rules would disappear by default, and agencies could not replace them for at least two years. Any repeal of rules would be allowed during the freeze, but no new protections.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals every federal rule that became effective after October 1, 1991, one year after enactment, unless Congress has specifically reauthorized it after that date — a default sunset covering roughly two decades of agency rules.

Imposes a moratorium on nearly all agency rulemaking — including proposed rules, policy statements, and even notices — lasting until the later of two years after enactment or two weeks after an OMB review report.

During the freeze, agencies may still act to repeal, narrow, or streamline rules once OMB certifies the action reduces regulatory burdens, and rules governing banks, tax collection, the military, and international trade agreements are excluded from the repeal and freeze.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the loss of the repealed rules — air and water standards, workplace and product safety rules, food safety requirements, and benefit and program rules all fall away by default, with each rule requiring an affirmative act of Congress to restore. Agencies would also spend their resources on an OMB-directed review of every rule instead of their normal work.

drawbacks.text: The default repeal is not selective: every rule in effect since 1991 — including public health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections — disappears unless Congress reauthorizes each one, and a rule that saved lives would be as much at risk as one that was obsolete.

The emergency valve is narrow: agencies cannot act on imminent dangers unless the head of the agency requests a waiver and the OMB Administrator signs off on a finding of an imminent threat to health or safety or other emergency.

Even supporters would acknowledge the disruption: reversing nearly 20 years of rules by default would create legal uncertainty for businesses and individuals who built plans around existing rules, and no private right of action exists to challenge violations of the freeze.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some businesses would benefit from less regulation, and a case-by-case review of old rules could be justified. But this bill does not review rules — it deletes them. The default is repeal of every federal rule issued since 1991, with the burden on Congress to rescue each one, and the carve-outs protect banking and tax rules while leaving health, safety, and environmental rules to fall. The costs to the public would be far larger and less certain than the gains to any particular industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees, which passed it down to subcommittees in late 2011, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young introduced the bill on October 13, 2011, and 17 Republican colleagues cosponsored it; all 18 were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors.

The House referred it to the Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary Committees, which assigned it to the Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law and the Subcommittee on Regulatory Affairs, Stimulus Oversight and Government Spending on October 24 and November 2, 2011.
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion movement — appears in the record, and the 112th Congress ended without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the existing body of federal protections, since the default repeal never took effect; businesses that hoped to shed regulation gained nothing, and the broad deregulation push behind the bill got no traction in either chamber.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and the bill never drew any Democratic support.

industries.industry: Heavily regulated manufacturers and energy, mining, and chemical firms
industries.note: The bill would have wiped out the environmental, workplace, and product safety rules these firms operate under, with no replacement rulemaking allowed for at least two years. The public would have absorbed the resulting pollution, safety, and health risks.

industries.industry: Banks and federally regulated financial institutions
industries.note: The bill carved banking regulators' rulemaking and existing financial rules out of both the repeal and the freeze, so banks faced neither the default deregulation other industries would have gotten nor new restrictions. Their regulatory regime would have stayed exactly as it was.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and the regulatory process itself
industries.note: Agencies would have been barred from issuing even proposed rules or policy notices for at least two years and required to assign Regulatory Review Officers to defend existing rules before Congress. Their protective function — which the public relies on — would have been suspended.
